messages.subject: [S] model of proportions
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

can someone enlighten me on the following or point me to the right
references where I can find out more about this?

Imagine, that I have a data set where the response variable is a
proportion (say the proportion of a volume) and with some explanatory
variable(s). The proportion of the response is not made up of several
entities (thus a classical logistic regression with 0s and 1s doesn't
work). [I also know that there are recent special methods to work with
compositional data e.g. developed by Peter Guttorp.] But let's assume for
the moment that I am either only interested in one component or that there
are only two components.

Now, I made up a simple example and tried two things:

Firstly, I fed the data into glm (Y ~ X, family= binomial). This seems to
give a sensible curve (though the tests might be wrong?) but the handbook
is very clear about that the binomial family expects only two different
values in the response. 

Secondly, I transformed Y into Z = log (Y/1-Y). Then I fitted a line by
lm (Z ~ X). If I look at the estimated values they are very similar
(though the tests of the coefficients are not).

What I don't see/understand is:
- How exactly are the two methods related (is the former just a least
  square and the latter a loglikelihood estimate)?
- Which of the two is (more?) correct?
- Is there a better way to do this with some "standard methods" (I am
  trying to give some advice to someone else for this)?
- What happens if I cover the whole range between 0 and 1 (including quite
  a few 0s and 1s)? E.g. I expect problems with the second version as
  I assume that the resiudals won't be normally distributed anymore. 

I am glad about any pointers or comments! Thank you for your time.

Regards, Lorenz

messages.body_plain:
Kim Pilegaard and I have been corresponding about the problem with
mixed.text() and mixed.mtext() that Kim encountered on a Solaris
installation (reported in a message last week).  We determined that
the problem was that a locale variable was set on Kim's machine
(LC_NUMERIC=da.ISO8859-15) that causes numbers to be written by awk
using a comma rather than a period as a decimal mark.  This can be
fixed by setting LC_NUMERIC=C before running S-Plus or by modifying
the function afm() so that the variable is reset before running the
awk command.  I pass this on for the benefit of other European users
who may be using this locale.

messages.subject: [S] model of proportion: summary of responses
messages.subject_clean: [S] model of proportion: summary of responses
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was asked to summarize to the list. Many thanks to Prof Brian Ripley,
James Pratt and Brian Cade who offered ideas and help! 

I was interested in how to correctly model proportions with a "standard" 
method. There were the following two things that I proposed:

Firstly, I fed the data into glm (Y ~ X, family= binomial).
Secondly, I transformed Y into Z = log (Y/1-Y). Then I fitted a line by
lm (Z ~ X).

Brian RIPLEY (ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk) pointed out, that glm (..., family=
binomial) does not expect zeros and ones in the response but: "The
`handbook' is wrong. It converts the response to a proportion." 

For my two propositions he clarifies: "Other way round. Actually, in your
case the second is least squares and the first is weighted least squares
with weights 1/(p*(1-p))".

Which one is more correct "Depends on how the proportions were measured".

And he advices me: "I would use glm with a quasi model logit link, and an
appropriate variance function (and you will need to work out what
appropriate is)."

Which will also help if there are many 0s and 1s: "log(Y/(1-Y)) will be
Inf or -Inf, and this will not work.  A quasi glm() model will work". 

James PRATT (jamesp at MOCR.OAPI.COM) proposed the same and pointed out a
reference (which can also be found in VR2):

"Have you tried quasilikelihood?  Logistic regression does assume a
binomial distribution for the errors.  With quasilikelihood, need only
define the variance function, but need not define a distribution.  In
McCullagh & Nelder 2nd edition, they give an example where response is the
percentage of a leaf's area affected by blotch.  This is example 9.2.4 on
page 328.  (In the 1st ed., the example is 8.6.1 on page 173). 

They first use a scaled version of the binomial variance (sigma*mu*(1-mu)) 
as the assumed variance function (with the logit link function for the
mean).  After some residual plots, they settle on using mu^2*(1-mu)^2, due
to scaled binomial variance function is too large at the extremes of 0 and
1. 

McCullagh & Nelder 'Generalized Linear Models' Chapman and Hall 1989 (2
ed), 1983 (1st ed)."

Brian CADE (Brian_Cade at usgs.gov) tends towards using a somewhat more
specialized method for dealing with compositional data:

"Perhaps you might want to work with the logratio approach advocated by
Aithchison for compositional data even though your testing and estimating
are focused on only 1 component.  Briefly, the logratio approach for a
2-part composition (call them y and z and say y is the component of
interest) would involve either of the following 2 transformations (maximal
invariants I believe): 
     
log(y/z)  or log(y/(y*z)^1/2).  The denominator in the first formula is
one of the indvidual components whereas in the second formual the
denominator is the geometric mean of the two components."

messages.body_plain:
I rec'd many useful messages re my request for a weighted multidimensional
scaling routine.

Doug Martin ,Doug Clarkson, Brian Ripley, Andreas Buja, Forrest Young
and Tim Johnson all replied.

 Here is a summary:

-Brian's isoMDS in the Splus library MASS does not take weights, but
 could be modified by incorporating wts in the monotone regression.
One would have to prove that this solves the wted problem.

-Forrest Young has a FORTRAN  routine ASCAL on his website
 http://forrest.psych.unc.edu

-Tim Johnson has an Splus routine for wted MDS on his website
http://www.psych.uiuc.edu/~tjohnson/tjohnson.html
based on  De Leeuw's (1977) SMACOF. I have already tried it and it seems
to work well!

-Andreas Buja pointed out his new MDS system xgvi.
The completed paper on the subject is in one of

xgvis.ps, xgvis.ps.gz, xgvis.pdf, xgvis.pdf.gz

from
 ftp://ftp.research.att.com/dist/xgobi/

-Finally, Jan De Leeuw has a superb paper 

Fitting distances by least squares

on his website

Thank you very much to everyone who helped out.

messages.subject: [S] Issues Regarding S-PLUS 5.0 Performance
messages.body_plain:
Recently, there have been several queries and postings 
regarding S-PLUS 5.0 and memory usage/performance 
issues.  This posting is intended to address these 
queries, and covers the following topics: 

1) Memory usage on start-up
2) General discussion of S-PLUS 5.0 (Release 3) performance
3) General programming tips

S-PLUS 5.0, Release 3 is now shipping to maintenance 
customers in North America. Going from Release 2 to 
Release 3, we have been able to significantly reduce 
memory usage and increase the speed of several 
important operations.   A high priority of the 
development team at MathSoft is to continue to improve 
the performance of S-PLUS 5.0. 

Memory Usage on Start-Up
------------------------

S-PLUS 5.0 appears to use more virtual memory on start-
up than does S-PLUS 3.4, but this appearance is 
misleading. As far as we can tell, there is relatively 
little difference in the actual memory available on 
startup to run your S-PLUS programs or other 
applications. 

If you use a utility such as "ps" or "top" on Solaris, 
it reports that S-PLUS 5.0 requires 48 megabytes of 
virtual memory (versus 8 megabytes for S-PLUS 3.4).  
What it doesn't tell you is that, of the 48 megabytes 
reported by Solaris, approximately 30 megabytes are in 
memory-mapped files that contain data, functions and 
other information S-PLUS needs to run. These files are 
memory-mapped to increase speed and to reduce the 
amount of real RAM used.   The 30 megabytes of memory-
mapped files do not appreciably reduce the amount of 
virtual memory available to other applications, or for 
other uses in S-PLUS. In addition, about 5 megabytes of 
the difference between 5.0 and 3.4 is in large common 
blocks in some FORTRAN code that is new to 5.0. This is 
never paged in unless that particular code is used but 
it does count against swap space. 

Discussion of S-PLUS 5.0, Release 3 (5.0R3) Performance
-------------------------------------------------------

S-PLUS 5.0 offers a new object-oriented model based on 
the latest generation S language from Lucent 
Technologies.  The new language significantly improves 
support for object-oriented programming in S-PLUS, 
expanding the scope of built-in data classes, providing 
explicit class structures with slots, supporting 
virtual classes, and improving the inheritance model.  
The new language also impacts performance in the 
following ways:

* Fewer copies of data objects are typically made 
during a function call in S-PLUS 5.0 compared to S-PLUS 
3.4.  This is due to reference counting, memory 
mapping, and use of the "copy" argument to calls to C 
and FORTRAN code.  This generally reduces memory 
requirements in S-PLUS 5.0.

* In 5.0R3, additional time is required to set-up 
function calls and more functions require more time-
consuming method invocation (since most low-level 
functions in S-PLUS 5.0 are generic).   This generally 
increases evaluation time when operating on small 
objects.

Almost everything S-PLUS does is a function call, and 
S-PLUS contains approximately 4,000 functions. 
Generalizations about a system as complex as S-PLUS are 
risky, but the following rules are useful:

* Functions applied to large data objects are generally 
faster and use less memory in 5.0R3 than in S-PLUS 3.4.   
As an example, our benchmarks indicate that lm() can 
handle data sets 2-3 times larger than in 3.4, and is 
faster for data sets larger than about 5,000-10,000 
observations.   

* Functions applied to small data objects are generally 
slower in 5.0R3 than in S-PLUS 3.4. In addition, 
looping is generally slower and uses more memory when 
there are many expressions and small data objects 
within the loop. This is due both to the overhead of 
small functions, and to the fact that 5.0R3 is not 
doing the same type of memory compaction within the 
loop (this is something we are looking at in our 
development effort).  Much of the difference in memory 
usage can be removed by encapsulating the contents of 
the loop within a single function call. 

General Programming Tips
------------------------

Our experience with S-PLUS 5.0 indicates that the 
following general programming tips are even more 
important in 5.0 than they were in 3.4:

(1) Use vectorized computations.
(2) Use apply, lapply, and related functions for 
looping computations wherever possible.
(3) Encapsulate the body of a loop in a single function 
call.

messages.body_plain:
Roger Koenker wrote
> Can someone suggest an efficient S-way to compute recursive least
> squares estimates, i.e.,
> 
>       p <- ncol(X)+1
>       T <- nrow(X)
>       bhat <- matrix(0,p,T)
>       for(t in (p+1):T){
>               bhat[,t] <- lm(y[1:t]~X[1:t,])$coef
>               }
> 
> I thought that there was a clever QR-decomposition trick...but I can't
> seem to find it.
> 
> 
> url:  http://www.econ.uiuc.edu                Roger Koenker   
> email roger at ysidro.econ.uiuc.edu              Department of Economics

(1) Run e.g.
R <- qr.R(cbind(1,x1,x2,,...,y))

(2) Let Rsubm be a submatrix of R consisting of the first m rows
and columns of R, and let zsubm be the vector of the first m
elements of the final column of R.  Then solve Rsubm b = y
to get the vector b of coefficients.

Watch out for the effects of pivoting, though.  It appears from
the documentation that qr.R() undoes any pivoting (see qr), but 
I've not checked this.

There are in addition ways to use lm(y~x1+x2+.., qr=T)$qr,
and then qr.coef
Basically you chop off as many trailing columns of the qr
representation as you do not want, before you call
qr.coef(qr,y)

With this approach, it is not obvious how you handle pivoting,
whereby the decomposition may be given for a version of X
in which columns are permuted.

CSIRO Mathematical & Information Sciences presents:

Analysing and Visualising Data

A two day Short Course plus a Workshop at Macquarie University, Sydney,
Australia
24th - 26th February 1999

Presented by Bill Cleveland, Bill Venables and Steve Davies

Don't miss out on this rare opportunity!  Bill Cleveland, currently at Bell
Labs US, is travelling to Australia especially to present this course.

Short Course 24 - 25 February 1999

Two decades of research in statistical graphics and data visualisation,
together with the revolution in computer graphics, have combined to produce
a new frontier of data analysis.  The course will present visualisation
tools that provide deep insight into the structure of data. Some tools, such
as q-q plots, are old standards.  Many other tools are new, and on the
leading edge of approaches to data visualisation.  One example is trellis
display, a framework for analysing multivariable data. Trellis provides the
most powerful mechanism yet developed for understanding interactions in
studies of how a response depends on explanatory variables.

But the material in the course is much more than a compendium of useful
tools.  It conveys an approach to data analysis that stresses the use of
visualisation to thoroughly study the structure of data and to check the
validity of statistical models fitted to data.  The result is a vast
increase in what can be learnt from data.

Who Should Attend the Short Course

The course is intended for anyone who has data to analyse.  The
prerequisites are familiarity with basic statistics and the least-squares
method of fitting equations to data.  For example, an introductory course in
statistics that included the fundamentals of regression analysis would be
sufficient. The content of the short course is not limited to S-PLUS
customers, users of any graphics software system can benefit.

Workshop 26 February 1999

Participants will put into practice the methods learnt during the short
course, using S-PLUS as the software tool. There will be particular emphasis
on trellis displays. All participants will be provided with a personal
computer for this session, and tutors will be constantly on hand to assist
with questions.  Some basic experience in using S-PLUS is essential for the
workshop.

Attend either the Short Course, or Workshop, or both.

I was asked to post summary, here it goes.
To add a link to a family you need to edit particular family.  I.E. for

function(link = "logit")

# This is a generator function for a family object
# To see a brief summary of the resulting family, 
# evaluate the function, e.g. binomial(), and let
# it print itself. To see individual components, either
# type binomial()$link etc., or else assign it and look at 
# the components.
        link <- as.character(substitute(link))
        misnames <- c("logit", "probit", "cloglog", "Logit", "Probit", 
                "clog-log", "Cloglog", "Clog-log")
        corresp <- c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3)
        lmatch <- pmatch(link, misnames, F)
        if(!lmatch)
                stop("Binomial links are \"logit\", \"probit\", or
\"cloglog\"; use \"quasi\" family for other links"
                        )
        link <- misnames[corresp[lmatch]]
        make.family("Binomial", glm.links[, link], glm.variances[,
"mu(1-mu"])
}

misnames, corresp, ...

It is a _restricted_ likelihood, based on fewer effective observations.
Use method="ml" to compare models. I think you will find lme() more
informative for such models, but you will need est.method="ML".

> mod1_varcomp(log(rep)~site,data,method="reml",tol=1e-10)
> 
> mod3_varcomp(log(rep)~plant+site,data,method="reml",tol=1e-10)
> 
> where log(rep) is the dependent var, site is a random factor, and plant is
> a quantitative independent variable (data is the name of the data frame).
> 
> I can get the likelihoods from mod1$info[7] and mod3$info[7]:
> 
> > mod1$info[7]
>  objective 
>  -8.652036
> > mod3$info[7]
>  objective 
>  -8.867806
> 
> This makes no sense to me at all - how can the likelihood for the more
> complex model be less?  Is there an error in the function, or am I being
> stupid here?

You need to know the likelihood of what: in this, lme (by default) and
arima.mle (which isn't using MLEs) the effective dataset changes with the
model.  REML uses the marginal likelihood of the residuals from a
least-squares fit of the fixed effects (grand mean +/- plant in your
example).

messages.body_plain:
> Date: Thu, 03 Dec 1998 06:59:51 -0600
> From: William Shannon <shannon at osler.wustl.edu>

> I felt the major deficiency of 3.4 was its inability to analyze large
> datasets. From the comments above it appears that 5.0 has reversed the
> problem -- it is now difficult to handle small datasets. Here is a

> The 5.0 requires 26 minutes to invert 10,000 3x3 matrices versus 3
> minutes with 3.4. There 'IS' a problem here that needs to be solved to
> make this product acceptable to people doing applied data analysis!

More precisely, it needs 26 minutes to do it THIS WAY.  I am not aware
of any `applied data analysis' problem on small datasets that requires
such a calculation, but if there is one, there are faster ways on
5.0r3, at least.  (BTW, I believe the posting of results from beta
software to be irresponsible.)

I ran a set of scripts for the V&R2 chapters last night, on my Sun
Ultra 1/170 with 64Mb RAM (sufficient) and 200Mb swap (ditto):

chapter  2    3     4    5     6    7    11   12   13  14
3.4r1   3.0  3.2    9.4 123  16.9   52  572  355  108  74
5.0r3   6.1  9.3  184  1201  77.2  266  840  522  141 322

I replaced step() by stepAIC() in all cases, as step() is seriously
broken in 5.0 and gives completely incorrect answers. The results from
chapters 5-14 are genuine applied data analysis of small datasets.

There appears to be a considerable speed penalty, especially when
running pure S code.  Note though that almost all of the statistical
models code in 5.0 is still running in compatibility mode, and one
would expect a drop in performance (if not this much). Would one
really notice?  Doing bootstrapping (ch05) and cross-validating 
trees (ch14), yes, so we need to think about improving those. Otherwise
the results are already fast enough for me: remember these are lots
of analyses per chapter. (Indeed they are much faster than 3.2 on a Sun
IPC which is how we first did most of the examples in 1992/3.)

I expect I will be using 3.4 for some time-consuming calculations for
a long time to come, but 5.0r3 is perfectly adequate for my routine
work (unlike 5.0r2, which used much more memory).

messages.subject: [S] SUMMARY: moving Trellis axis labels closer
messages.subject_clean: [S] SUMMARY: moving Trellis axis labels closer
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

(all the following applies to S-Plus 3.4 and 5.0r2 for Solaris)

a really looooooooong time ago (in August) I posted the 
following query:

|> I want to move the x and y labels on an xyplot (containing
|> but a single panel) closer to their axes than the default.
|> 
|> Unfortunately, setting  par(mgp=c(1.5, 0.5, 0))  does not
|> seem to change anything.
|> xyplot also won't accept  mgp=c(1.5, 0.5, 0)  as an argument

Thanks to Patrick Conolly who suggested to put mgp in the
'scales=' argument of trellis calls, but unfortunately that
won't help either:

Apparently the internal workhorse function render.trellis()
(which is called by print.trellis()) uses only 
par("mgp")[2], the first value (which places the label) is ignored.

>>From my reverse engineering effort it seems that you can't really
move the label closer unless you change the render.trellis() code,
because Trellis does a really stupid thing: it creates an internal
_fixed_ 0.2 inch gap between tick marks and axis label.
This is quite silly for small plots (such as 3 by 4 inch, which 
I use frequently), because it wastes a large amount of plotting 
area.

Here is what I found:

print.trellis() 
calls  render.trellis()
which computes labs.line
which is later passed on to do.page()
which calls do.mtext(line=labs.line[i])
which calls mtext(...)

The computation of labs.line is as follows:
        ex <- e/do.cin.trellis(scale.x$cex)[2]
        ey <- e/do.cin.trellis(scale.y$cex)[2]
        sline <- do.line(do.cin.trellis(xlab$cex)[2], scale.x$cex) + ex
        labs.line <- c(do.line(omi.axes[1], scale.x$cex) + ex, 
                       do.line(omi.axes[2], scale.y$cex) + ey, 
                       do.line(omi.axes[3], scale.x$cex) + ex + 
                mline, do.line(omi.axes[1], scale.x$cex) + ex + sline)
        par(omi = omi.axes + e + omi + 0.2)
where e is set as
        e <- 0.2 # gap between labels in inch
farther above.
As a quick fix, we can make two changes: 
the value of e and the 0.2 in the par(omi=) call
        e <- 0.04  # 2mm
        par(omi = omi.axes + e + omi + 0.04)
The latter just saves some more wasted space at the edges.
I've used fix(render.trellis) for the change, hence the result will
be local to one working directory only.

I wonder why trellis does not just use par("mgp")[1] instead?

  Lutz

messages.subject: [S] loops in likelihood in Gaussian mixtures
messages.subject_clean: [S] loops in likelihood in Gaussian mixtures
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I need help with how to avoid the following loop.

I'm trying to calculate the likelihood of some data.  The likelihood
function for each data point is a mixture of K weighted normals, i.e.
P(y|\theta)=\sum_i^K w_i normal(y).
The problem is that not only K has to vary, say, randomly  between
1-10, the parameters for the normal, mu and sigma, all need to be
different for each K. The likelihood gets stored in an array, P.

The solution with loops is straight forward: 

N_100                  # number of data points
data_rgamma(N,8)       # some random data, a vector
K_ceiling(runif(1)*10) # number of mixture components, randomly chosen
P_rep(0,N)             # likelihood
w_runif(K)             # get some weights
w_w/sum(w)             # normalize the weights
mu_runif(K)            # pick K mean/std for the mixture components
sigma_runif(K)

for(n in 1:length(data))            # loop through each data point
 for(i in 1:K)                      # loop through each mixture component
   P[n]_P[n]+w[i]*dnorm(data[n],mu[i], sigma[i]);   # compute the likelihood

I don't know how to vectorize the operation that, given one data
point, K mu and K sigma, returns an array of corresponding K
probabilities. Can apply be somehow made to work? Ideally, one hopes
to get something like sum(w*dnorm(data[n], mu, sigma)).

Secondly I wonder if there is a way to vectorize the above operation over
the entire data set with N data points.

Thanks so much in advance.

fei

messages.subject: [S] multifactors for Trellis?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

if one wants to have multiple panels showing different subsets
of the data in Trellis, one has two possibilities
 - use a factor:
   This gives arbitrary subsets, but they are always disjoint
 - use a shingle:
   This gives subsets that may overlap, but each one is always
   a contiguous numerical region (an interval)

Is there any way to get arbitrary subsetting, i.e.,
something as flexible as a factor, but where each element
may appear more than once?

Example:
I have the datapoints 1,2,3,4,5 and would like to get one
panel with 1,2, one with 3,4,5, and one with, say, 1,2,4,
in it.

One can of course do this in multiple plots, but this is cumbersome
and also loses many of the specific Trellis advantages 
such as common axis ranges etc.

((An appropriate data structure would be a boolean matrix with
one column per subset and as many rows as the corresponding
dataframe. Or one could have a more space-efficient representation
using an integer (the number of subsets) and a function which
returns a boolean subscription vector when given the number of
a subset.))

It seems to me that this may be impossible to achive directly
with a single Trellis high level call.

Or, is it?

Where would one have to change Trellis in order to
add such functionality?
Unfortunately, the Trellis code is sadly uncommented and
hard to get through.

Subject: [S] Persp() questions

Among other questions about producing perspective plots using the `persp'
function, Jonathan Stroud (jon at stat.duke.edu) asks:

>  (2) When using the function persp(), the z-axis labels are often crowded
>  or overlapping.  What can I do to fix this?

I encountered this problem a few years ago and recall that it took a small
army of skilled (and ultimately traumatized) people to resolve it.
The solution went something like this:

If you type  persp  at the S-Plus prompt, you obtain the (ascii) definition
of the persp function.  It is necessary to change the definition of the
function; let's call the new function  `mpersp'.  Place the ascii
definition of persp into a file and change the function as follows:

The first two lines of the persp function are:

function(x, y, z, xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", zlab = "Z", axes = T, box = T, eye = 
        NULL, zlim, ar = 1, ...)

It is necessary to make a small change to the second line as follows:

function(x, y, z, xlab = "X", ylab = "Y", zlab = "Z", axes = T, box = T, eye = 
        NULL, zlim, zticks = 3, ar = 1, ...)

Next, locate each of the two lines of the persp function which read as:

        rangez <- expand.range(pretty(z))
and
        rangez <- expand.range(pretty(zlim))

and change these to:

        rangez <- expand.range(pretty(z, zticks))
and
        rangez <- expand.range(pretty(zlim, zticks))

respectively.

Now read in this new `mpersp' function definition into your S-Plus.

A typical S-Plus calling sequence to the new function might look as follows:

mpersp ( x=a.grid, y=b.grid,
         z=FFT2D,
         zticks=3,
         xlab = "\n\na",  ylab="\n\nb", zlab="solution\n" )

The choice `zticks = 3' can be changed throughout as required.

biases in always rounding 0.5 up or always down.  Try reading the help

       When rounding off a 5, the two common conventions are  to:
       1)  go  to  the higher number, or 2) go to the even digit.
       The round function obeys convention 2, so round(2.5) is  2
       and  round(3.5) is 4. The rounding mechanism for signif is
       machine dependent, but most machines will use  the  "round
       to even" rule.

This is a definite FAQ - this is the 4th time in the last 4 months.
Here are several solutions:

(1) for a single Greek character: use the "symbol" font (Font 13 on Unix
systems, I don't know about the PCs).

(2) if it suits your needs and you are on a PC, use the graph editing
features.

(3) if you need to mix fonts up in one label, use my "postscriptfonts"
archive from Statlib. These functions allow you to create simple to
moderately complex labels using a string with escape sequences for change
of font, super and subscripts, change of size, etc.  Takes some fiddling
to make it beautiful but it works entirely within S-plus.

(4) use the "psfrag" utilities (there are a few variations around) that
work with LaTeX or TeX, so you can create the label in those languages and
have them appear within a PostScript plot.  THe way to go for truly
high-quality typesettnig, but requires some additional steps.

messages.subject: [S] Cox model for grouped data
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

I want to estimate a Cox proportional hazards model with S-Plus.
The characteristics of my data are the following ones:

1. heavyly cenrosed sample: I have about 2737 subjects and just 150 events.

2. grouped data: data are grouped by year. That is, I have data on my 
dependent variable and the covariates at the end of every year. 

3. ties: as a consequence of the discrete character of my data
I have many ties some of the years.

4. not all the subjects enter the risk set at the
same time.

5. time dependent covariates: several of my covariates change their
value every year.

6. observation window: 10 years.

My concern mainly relates to the way of handling this grouped version
of the Cox proportional hazards model. On the one hand I do not want
to use the logistic approximation of the model, but the true Cox model.
On the other I do not know if it is possible to implement the Prentice and 
Gloeckler (1978) version of the model in S-Plus and I am not sure if the
counting process version of Andersen and Gill (1982) is appropriate for my
case. I have the same doubts about the method (Efron, Breslow, exact)
I should use for handling ties.

Suggestions are welcome.

Thanks a lot.

Jaime Gomez.

University of Zaragoza.

Thanks to Brian Ripley (without whose sometimes testy comments this list
would probably die, or at least lose a lot of its utility), Sam Buttrey,
John Wallace,  John Fennick, and Scott Chasalow.

Question 1: Why does grep work this way?
grep("*ABC*", "ABC123456789")
 [1] 1
  grep("*ABC*", "ABC123456789/")                # Only difference is the slash
 numeric(0)
 
Answer 1: grep has a bug under Splus 3.3; there are some ways around it
provided you know it is there (see one below).  Brian Ripley reports "In
fact the whole of grep on Windows seems to be a bug, as it does not match
regular expressions."  

Question 2.  does anybody have a function that will find the POSITION of a
string in a vector of larger strings (or 0 if not there)?

 The question wasn't clear.  WHat I meant was, given
x <- c("abcdefghi", "lmnop", "defabc")
I would like a function that figures out where in each element a given text
string is, sort of an inverse of substring:
whatfunction(x, "def")
[1] 4 0 1

Answer 2: Brian recommends upgrading to 4.x and using regexpr , but for me
this falls in the "if it ain't broke" category provided not too many of
these bugs appear.  I tried upgrading when 4.0 came out but it was too
frustrating.  Version 3.3 is much newer than my car, too, and I will keep
driving THAT until it dies.

WOrkaround for question 1, courtesy of John Wallace:

grep("*ABC*", get.subs("ABC123456789/", sep="/"))

"get.subs" <- function(x, sep = ",")
{
#   DATE WRITTEN:  26 May 1995, Revised 28 Feb. 1996
#   Author:  John R. Wallace (jw at u.washington.edu)
#
        if(length(sep) == 1) sep <- substring(sep, 1:nchar(sep),
                1:nchar(sep))
        nc <- nchar(x)
        y <- (1:nc)[is.element(substring(x, 1:nc, 1:nc), sep)]
        if(is.na(y[1] + 0))
                return(x)
        substring(x, c(1, y + 1), c(y - 1, nc))
}

messages.body_plain:
(FAO Wim Kemmerer):

Re a routine for string searches:

I use the following function 'pos' to locate substrings. On the plus side, it 
is entirely written in S-plus, so it's portable; on the minus side, it can be 
pretty slow. Either the string searched for, or the string searched in, can be 
a vector of length > 1. "pos" returns a numeric matrix as output, as the 
following examples show:

pos_ function(substrs, mainstrs, any.case = F, names.for.output) <<code at end 
of email>>

Examples:

> pos( 'at', 'the cat in the hat')
[,1] [,2] 
[1,]    6   17
Vector of length 2, because 'at' appears twice.

> pos( 'at', 'does not appear here')
[,1]
[1,] 0
Vectors returned are always of length at least 1; 0 means no match. You can use 
"pos( x, y)[1]>0" to test if x is found at all within y.

> pos( 'oo', 'xoooo')
     [,1] [,2] [,3] 
[1,]    2    3    4
Note the overlap here.

> pos( 'at', c( 'cat', 'catcat', 'balloon'))
[,1] [,2] 
[1,]    2    0
[2,]    2    5
[3,]    0    0
This is a 2x3 matrix: the 3 because there are 3 elements to "mainstrs", and the 
2 because "substrs" occurs at most twice in any element of "mainstrs". Each row 
shows the successive occurences of "substrs" within the corresponding element 
of "mainstrs".

> pos( c( 'at', 'the', 'back', 'Jack'), 'there is standing room at the back')
     [,1] [,2] 
[1,]   24    0
[2,]    1   27
[3,]   31    0
[4,]    0    0
This time the rows correspond to elements of  "substrs" not "mainstrs".

> pos( c( 'at', 'the'), 'nowhere')
[,1] 
[1,]    0
[2,]    0
as you might expect.

If both "substrs" and "mainstrs" are length>1, "pos" tries to replicate the 
shorter one to be the same length as the longer, and then checks substr[1]  
against mainstr[1], substr[2] against mainstr[2], etc., returning each result 
as the row of a matrix. There will be a warning message of the "Length of 
longer not a multiple of length of shorter" variety if applicable.

>pos( c( 'at', 'the'), c( 'the', 'quick'))
[,1]
[1,] 0
[2,] 0
because 'at' doesn't match 'the', and 'the' doesn't match 'quick'.

The "any.case" argument puts everything into upper case before looking for 
matches.

If "substrs" and "mainstrs" are not of the same length, the names (if any) of 
the longer will be the row.names of the output matrix. If there are no names, 
the row names won't be provided. You can override these behaviours by supplying 
the "names.for.output" argument; it must be the same length as the longer of 
"substrs" or "mainstrs".

NB that if you know you're looking for single characters, you may find the 
function "AsciiToInt" useful. This breaks a string into a numeric vector of 
ascii codes. In version 4.0, this has been upgraded into the a function 
"string.to.chars" which is quicker than "substring( x, 1:nchar(x), 1:nchar( 
x)). 

Code follows. Note you need the function "upper.case" (defined at the end) as 
well.

Hope this helps--

Mark Bravington
m.v.bravington at cefas.co.uk

pos_ function(substrs, mainstrs, any.case = F, names.for.output)
{
  ls <- length(substrs)
  lm <- length(mainstrs)
  .pos <- function(substr, mainstr)
  {
    ns <- nchar(substr)
    nm <- nchar(mainstr)
    if(ns > nm)
      return(0)
    mainstr <- substring(mainstr, 1:(nm - ns + 1), ns:nm)
    t <- (1:length(mainstr))[mainstr == substr]
    if(length(t) == 0)
      0
    else t
  }
  if(any.case) {
    substrs <- upper.case(substrs)
    mainstrs <- upper.case(mainstrs)
  }
  if((ls == 1) && (lm == 1))
    return(matrix(.pos(substrs, mainstrs), 1))
  if((ls %% lm) * (lm %% ls))
    warning( "Length of longer not a multiple of length of shorter")
  if(ls < lm) {
    if(missing(names.for.output))
      names.for.output <- names(mainstrs)
    substrs <- rep(substrs, (lm %/% ls) + 1)
  }
  else if(ls > lm) {
    if(missing(names.for.output))
      names.for.output <- names(substrs)
    mainstrs <- rep(mainstrs, (ls %/% lm) + 1)
  }
  else if(missing(names.for.output))
    names.for.output <- names(mainstrs)
  ls <- max(ls, lm)
  j <- vector("list", ls)
  for(i in (1:ls))
    j[[i]] <- .pos(substrs[i], mainstrs[i])
  max.n.pos <- max(sapply(j, length))
  if(max.n.pos == 1)
    jj <- matrix(unlist(j), 1)
  else {
    jj <- sapply(j, function(x, w)
    c(x, rep(0, w - length(x))), w = max.n.pos)
  }
  dimnames(jj) <- list(character(0), names.for.output)
  t(jj)
}

messages.subject: [S] Survfit output
messages.body_plain:
I have posted earlier this week a question on how print.survfit gives the
result:

It seems that the problem is: 

print.survfit orders the categories in the order of absolute value of
leading character:

So the following is the  order in which print.survfit would give the result:
1)
                n events mean se(mean) median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL 
xcat=0+ thru 1 20     17 7.22    2.007   2.92    1.53    9.41
xcat=1+ thru 2 30     18 5.31    0.781   5.55    2.35    9.93

As any other function.
 xcat=0+ thru 1 xcat=1+ thru 2 
             20             30

2)HOWEVER when the leading character is -1 the result appears:

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(survtime, status) ~ xcat)
 
                 n events mean se(mean) median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL 
xcat= 0+ thru 2 30     18 5.31    0.781   5.55    2.35    9.93
xcat=-1+ thru 0 20     17 7.22    2.007   2.92    1.53    9.41

when other S-plus functions would give the result in this order:
 xcat=-1+ thru 0 xcat= 0+ thru 2 
              20              30

The slution which I found and which seems to work is after using the
function cut , to attach lebels to the categories:
xcat_cut(x-1,c(-1,0,2),label=c('1','2'))

In this way the result appears:

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(survtime, status) ~ xcat)
 
        n events mean se(mean) median 0.95LCL 0.95UCL 
xcat=1 20     17 7.22    2.007   2.92    1.53    9.41
xcat=2 30     18 5.31    0.781   5.55    2.35    9.93

Which is the same order as for other functions
 xcat=1 xcat=2 
     20     30

Thank you to all those who spent time on this problem.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Offsets in Poisson regression
messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "Simon," == Simon, Steve, PhD <ssimon at cmh.edu> writes:

    Simon> How does one properly specify an offset variable for
    Simon> glm() using a Poisson family? The HELP file tells me
    Simon> that the offset() function "is not intended to be
    Simon> called directly by users." 

The common case is for the poisson mean to have a known factor,
say variable N, in which case for a log-linear model the fit
would take the form

fit.mod <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + offset(log(N)), poisson, dat, .....)

I suggest the advice that the function offset() should not be
called directly by users has to be understood as meaning that you
only use it in this unique context.  In fact this is a so-called
"special" function recognized in glm model formulae (but not lm
or aov, curiously) and it is not actually evaluated at all, but
used to specify a fixed part of the linear predictor.  Other
special functions for other purposes include Error() for aov
model formulae and strata() for survfit models.

    Simon> Also, I can't find any good examples in the S-plus 4
    Simon> Guide to Statistics or in the Venables and Ripley
    Simon> book.

I cannot speak for the first, but for the second publication such
an example is under construction.  If there is a huge demand I
may suggest to my colleague we weave it into the complements, but
it is not such an immense deal, really.

    Simon> I'm using version 4.5 under Windows NT if that makes
    Simon> a difference.

I believe not.  This is part of the common heritage.

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Offsets in Poisson regression
messages.body_plain:
> How does one properly specify an offset variable for glm() using a Poisson
> family? The HELP file tells me that the offset() function "is not intended
> to be called directly by users." 

The offset() help message is pretty unhelpful; all it means is that 
offset() is meaningful only within a formula.

Simple example:

        glm(y~x+offset(z),family=poisson(),data=my.data.frame)

The first argument is the formula argument to glm.
This corresponds to a model of the form

        y ~ Poisson(lambda)
        log(lambda) = beta0 + beta1*x + z

where beta0 and beta1 are coefficients to be estimated.

>>>>> Mikio Kaihara <mkaihara at ichinoseki.ac.jp> writes:
:  
:  Dear S(S-PLUS)users, I would like to generally bind N columes
:  (mat1, mat2, mat3, ..., matN) as columes of a Matrix(see the
:  concrete example below).
:  
:  > A <- mat1
:  > A <- cbind(A,mat2)
:  > A <- cbind(A,mat3)
:  > A
:            [,1]        [,2]        [,3] 
:  [1,] 0.4086589 -0.07046737 -0.07763975
:  [2,] 0.4208061 -0.25675230 -0.72808987
:  
:  Plese teach me how to express generally,in using "for (i in 1:N){}".

The natural ways to do it are not using for() loops, it seems to
me.  Here are a couple of ways that generalize to an arbitrary
number of matrices.

Suppose we start off with a couple of vectors with regularly
generated names:

> mat1 <- 1
> mat2 <- 1:2
> mat3 <- 2:3
> mat4 <- 1:4

1. Put the components into a list and use do.call:

> do.call("cbind", lapply(paste("mat",1:4,sep=""), get))
     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] 
[1,]    1    1    2    1
[2,]    1    2    3    2
[3,]    1    1    2    3
[4,]    1    2    3    4

2. Construct the call as a character string, parse it and evaluate:

> txt <- paste(c("cbind(", 
+                paste("mat", 1:4, sep = "", collapse = ","),
+                ")"), collapse = "")
> txt           # check!
[1] "cbind(mat1,mat2,mat3,mat4)"

> eval(parse(text=txt))
     mat1 mat2 mat3 mat4 
[1,]    1    1    2    1
[2,]    1    2    3    2
[3,]    1    1    2    3
[4,]    1    2    3    4

3. Do the same thing by more direct methods (ie not using parse()):

> txt <- c("cbind", paste("mat", 1:4, sep = ""))
> mode(txt) <- "expression"
> txt <- as.call(lapply(txt, as.name))
> txt           # check!
cbind(mat1, mat2, mat3, mat4)
> eval(txt)
     mat1 mat2 mat3 mat4 
[1,]    1    1    2    1
[2,]    1    2    3    2
[3,]    1    1    2    3
[4,]    1    2    3    4
> 

4. False method using a for() loop:

> M <- mat1
> for(i in 2:4) M <- cbind(M, get(paste("mat", i, sep=""))) # FAILS!

This will only work if all the components, mat2, mat3, ... are
all of the same length.  As they are not in this case, it fails.  

It is also not good form to be growing an object in this way
within a loop from an efficiency point of view, though in this
trivial case it hardly matters!

messages.subject: [S] Challenges and Successes in Teaching S-Plus and Graphics
messages.subject_clean: [S] Challenges and Successes in Teaching S-Plus and Graphics
messages.body_plain:
I just completed teaching a 2 semester hour course "Statistical
Computing and Graphics".  The students were primarily graduate
students in our M.S. in Health Evaluation Sciences program, plus 3
very quantitative undergraduate students (who all made As).  The
students had had a single stat/probability course previously.  The
texts are "An Introduction to S-Plus and the Hmisc and Design
Libraries" by Alzola and Harrell (available from our web page), "The
Elements of Graphing Data" by Bill Cleveland, and the S-Plus 4.5
Student Edition manual.  Students supplemented these texts with a
handout from Venables, with Venables & Ripley, and with the 3 Tufte
books.  The detailed syllabus may be found in
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat/teaching/statcomp.pdf.

Here is a summary of successes and challenges in teaching this course.
The biggest challenges, related to item 1 below, were teaching the
students the different modes of operating on data frames (creating /
modifying them vs. reading them) and teaching them the difference
between attributes of the whole data frame and attributes of its
constiuent variables.  Any help would really be appreciated for the
next time I teach the course, and perhaps some of these findings will
help other instructors.  For item 1, I am going to make a one-page
cheat sheet for the students to keep by them at all times.  This sheet
will contain a template for creating and modifying data frames.

Challenges

1.  attach, detach, use of $ prefix, when to quote a data frame name

 Students could never keep straight the fact that a data frame does
 not need to be in position 1 just to be analyzed, that it often
 needs to be in position 1 to be modified (without using the $
 prefix), that a program containing twenty $ prefixes is an
 inefficient use of their time.  They often forgot that detaching
 and saving a data frame from position one requires the data frame
 name to be in quotes (e.g., detach(1,'mydf')), sometimes wrecking
 their _Data.
 Oddly enough, most students seemed to understand the search list
 well, but couldn't tie it to other things.

2. Multiple variables by the same name

 Students would create variables outside of data frames (in the search
 position 1 _Data area) that would later override variables in data
 frames attached in search position 2.  When prompted, they would
 do find(), search(), etc., but would never remember how to track
 down the masking.  Luckily, most masking resulted in an S-Plus
 length mismatch error message.

3. Changing names of variables in a data frame

 Students had trouble renaming columns in a data frame.
 Often, students attempted to change "outer" attributes of a data
 frame while the data frame was attached.  I had to keep stressing
 to them that this should be done before any attaching.  Students
 would do names(dataframename) <- 'age' to re-name a single
 variable.  They seemed to have the most luck with
 names(dataframename) <- edit(names(dataframename)), although they
 sometimes edited in illegal names.

3. Defining or changing factor variables

 Lots of confusion between levels and labels in factor() function.
 And students often tried to run a factor variable back through the
 factor function, using the wrong vector of levels, resulting in
 NAs.  Once a factor variable was created properly, the students
 had little trouble using it.  But creating factor variables really
 confused the students.

4. Creating small datasets vs. importing dat

 We used expand.grid to allow students to input data from published
 tables into S-Plus for the purpose of converting the table to a
 graphic.  Many students could not understand expand.grid's
 input arguments.  Also, once a data frame was created, whether by
 expand.grid or by a function such as the Hmisc summarize function
 (which computes stratified descriptive statistics on variables and
 stores them in a data frame) students often forgot the
 data=dataframename argument to trellis functions.  Students seemed
 to be clear on importing data and "sticking with" the resulting
 data frame throughout an analysis, but got confused when data
 frames were created later in the process.

5. Commands vs. GUI

 I try to teach both approaches as I want the students to be able
 to come back to S-Plus when they have put it down for a while (the
 menus help here) as well as to be able to use the more flexible
 commands.  Mixing the two approaches really didn't cause much of a
 problem for the students.  It was more a problem for the
 instructor (changing gears, where to place emphasis).  One area in
 which the GUI-based interactive graphics was slightly frustrating
 was in editing graphics details (fonts, symbols associated with
 factor levels, etc.).

 One student who had no difficulty with any aspect of the command
 language was a student who had completed 3 programming courses
 (including C++).  He could easily come up with multiple solutions to
 each problem requiring use of the command line.

Successes

1. S-Plus 4.5 Student Edition

 The only problem we had using the Student Edition was the lateness
 of its arrival.  I found its manual to be quite well written, and
 the students seemed to really profit from this book.

2. Graphics

 Of course the students loved the graphics, and as always, Bill
 Cleveland's book was wonderful.  The 2D and 3D graphics pallettes
 worked well, especially in conjunction with dragging different
 conditioning variables from the object browser.

3. Projects using Student's Choice of Dataset

 Students were most stimulated when they chose their own data for
 an end-of-semester project.  Students got excellent data from
 Statlib, the Data and Story Library, and from other classes or
 from their jobs.  Our web page also has some good datasets.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Director, Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Dept of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://www.med.virginia.edu/medicine/clinical/hes/biostat.htm

messages.subject: [S] for() and process variance
messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

I would like to compute the process variance as defined in Diggle, Liang
& Zeger (1994), Analysis of longitudinal data, p.51:

sigma^2 = mean( .5 * (y_ij - y_mk)^2 ),
with i, m indices for subjects (i != m),
     j, k indices for time

I wrote the following small function, but could not find a way to avoid
the for() loop:

process.variance <- function(subj, resp){
  lst <- unique(subj)
  sq  <- 0
  n   <- 0
  for(i in 1:length(lst)){
    cond <- subj==lst[i]
    v <- as.vector(outer(resp[cond], resp[!cond], function(x,y)
.5*(x-y)^2))            
    sq <- sq + sum(v)
    n  <- n  + length(v)
    }
    sq / n
}

Would someone teach me how to do it better ?
I am working with S+ 4.5r3 for Win95.

Many thanks in advance and happy new year from Senegal !

Renaud
